explanations.answer: Finished stones for the house of God
explanations.explanation: David appointed stonecutters from the foreigners in the land of Israel to prepare finished stones for building the house of God. So the stones got shaped before anyone started stacking them. That's the kind of work nobody claps for. I can respect a man who gets the dough ready before the oven is even hot.

Walls for a city is a fair guess, friend, because stonecutters do cut for walls. But this verse names a different job. David had them prepare finished stones for building the house of God (1 Chronicles 22:2). The passage doesn't mention walls at all.

Solomon, David's son, is the reason for a lot of this planning, so I see why you went there. But the stones weren't for a palace. The text says David had them prepared for building the house of God. It's a house for the LORD, not a house for the kid.

I'm sorry, friend, but that little bit of bronze never happened. David provided more bronze than could be weighed. Nobody puts bronze on a scale and gives up because the scale quit. When the text says it can't be weighed, picture a LOT of bronze.

That's right, friend. The text says David provided a large quantity of iron, together with more bronze than could be weighed. That's no little bit. My kitchen scale would take one look at that pile and ask for a transfer.

Yes, friend. The text says the Sidonians and Tyrians brought David more cedar logs than could be counted. That's a pile past counting. I lose count on a long day of cookie batches, and mine only go up to about forty.

Carrying those logs sounds like real work, and somebody did bring them to David. But the text says something else about the number. It says there were more cedar logs than could be counted (1 Chronicles 22:4). The counting is what gave out.

Stacking them would be a job and a half, I'll give you that. The text doesn't say stacking, though. It says the Sidonians and Tyrians, people from Sidon and Tyre, brought more cedar logs than could be counted (1 Chronicles 22:4). The pile was past counting.

That's it, friend. David says, "My son Solomon is young and inexperienced…" Solomon is David's son, and David looks at the size of the job and says he must make preparations. I think that's a dad who knows his son has a long road ahead and wants to make it a little easier.

I get why it might sound like a fit, but that's not what David says. He calls Solomon "…young and inexperienced…" Nothing in this passage calls him proud or stubborn. David talks like a dad who sees how big the job is, and I think he's worried about it.

Bold and ready is nice to hear, but David doesn't say it. He says Solomon is "…young and inexperienced…" That's why David says he must make preparations. If Solomon were already ready, I don't think David would be hauling in all those logs.

You got it, friend. David says the house to be built for the LORD must be "…exceedingly magnificent—famous and glorious throughout all lands." Then he adds, "Therefore I must make preparations for it."

That one trips people, but David did say it. His words are that the house to be built for the LORD must be "…exceedingly magnificent—famous and glorious throughout all lands." So the standard was set high from the start. David wanted this one done right.

explanations.answer: He has shed so much blood
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, friend. The LORD told David, "You have shed much blood and waged great wars." He added that David was not to build the house because he had shed so much blood on the ground before Him. It's a hard word to hear, and I think it hurt, even though David had it in his heart to build.

explanations.answer: He is too old to finish it
explanations.explanation: That's a reasonable guess, but age isn't what the LORD gives. His reason was that David had shed much blood and waged great wars. Nothing here says David was too old. The LORD's word to David spells out the blood as the reason.

explanations.answer: He has not asked the priests
explanations.explanation: It sounds like a sensible rule, but the priests don't come up in the LORD's word to David. The reason the LORD gave was, "You have shed much blood and waged great wars." That's the whole explanation in this passage. No one else is blamed for the answer.

Yes, friend. The LORD said the son would be "…a man of rest." The LORD would give him rest from all his enemies on every side. After a king with great wars behind him, a son of rest is quite the change.

War is what David knew, so I see where you went. But the LORD said David had waged great wars, and then He said the coming son would be a man of rest. The son was meant to be different from his father in that way (1 Chronicles 22:8-9). Rest is the word.

Sorrows doesn't show up anywhere in what the LORD told David about this son. He said the son would be "…a man of rest." He also said He would give him rest from all his enemies on every side. It's a hopeful word, friend.

That's it, friend. God said, "…I will grant to Israel peace and quiet during his reign." That's a promise worth hearing. David had waged great wars (1 Chronicles 22:8), so I bet peace and quiet sounded GOOD.

There's plenty of treasure in this passage, so I see why you reached for riches. But that's not what God promised for the son's reign. He said, "…I will grant to Israel peace and quiet during his reign." The gold and silver are David's preparations, not God's promise here.

A bigger army would make sense in a kingdom that has seen war. But God promised something different. He said He would give the son rest from all his enemies on every side and grant Israel "…peace and quiet…" That's the promise God gave about the reign.

I'm sorry, friend, but God's promise reaches way past one lifetime. He said, "…I will establish the throne of his kingdom over Israel forever." The word is forever, not a few years. Solomon, David's son, got a promise that outlasts him.
You've got it, friend. God said, "…I will establish the throne of his kingdom over Israel forever." That doesn't stop when Solomon does. It's a promise much bigger than one man's years.

Right, friend. David tells Solomon, "Above all, may the LORD give you insight and understanding when He puts you in command over Israel…" Solomon, David's son, has a big job coming. David puts insight and understanding above all.

With all that gold and silver lying around, wealth is an easy guess. But David doesn't wish it for Solomon. His wish is that the LORD would give Solomon insight and understanding when He puts him in command over Israel (1 Chronicles 22:12). The treasure was already gathered, and David's "above all" goes to understanding.

Victory in battle fits a king, but David doesn't wish for it here. His wish is that the LORD would give Solomon insight and understanding. The LORD had already said the son would be a man of rest (1 Chronicles 22:9). And David's "above all" goes to understanding.

Yes, friend. David wants Solomon to have insight and understanding "…so that you may keep the Law of the LORD your God." Understanding is for the keeping. Knowing is good, but David wants Solomon doing it too.

The house is a big part of this whole passage, so I see the pull. But David's reason for insight and understanding is different. It's "…so that you may keep the Law of the LORD your God." The house is the job. The Law is what he's meant to keep.

Land does come up later in this passage, but not here. David asks for insight and understanding so that Solomon may keep the Law of the LORD his God. The Law is the point of that wish. Solomon had a huge job, and David wanted his heart pointed the right way.

That's David's word, friend. He tells Solomon, "Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid or discouraged." Solomon, David's son, is young and facing a very big job. I think a dad saying that is hoping his boy hears it loud and clear.

That would be a cautious dad, but David doesn't say it. Right after pointing Solomon to the commands of the LORD, he says, "Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid or discouraged." David is pushing him toward the work, not away from it. He even says, "Now begin the work…" (1 Chronicles 22:16).

David does order the leaders of Israel to help Solomon, so I see the guess. But that isn't what he says to Solomon here. He tells him, "Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid or discouraged." That order to the leaders comes later (1 Chronicles 22:17), and Solomon is still the one being told to be strong.

That's not how David tells it, friend. He says, "…I have taken great pains to provide for the house of the LORD…" Great pains is not a light afternoon. That pile of gold, silver, bronze and iron cost him real work.
You've got it, friend. David says, "…I have taken great pains to provide for the house of the LORD…" That pile of gold, silver, bronze and iron wasn't gathered easily.

That's right, friend. David says the craftsmen in gold and silver, bronze and iron are "beyond number." He also tells Solomon, "You also have many workers…" (1 Chronicles 22:15). Solomon, David's son, isn't short on skilled hands.

Twelve is a nice neat number, but David doesn't give one. He says the craftsmen skilled in gold and silver, bronze and iron are "beyond number." So you can't count them on your fingers. Nobody can count them at all.

A handful would be a worry for a job this big. But David says the opposite. He says there are craftsmen "beyond number" skilled in gold and silver, bronze and iron. Solomon has plenty of help waiting.

You've got it, friend. David tells the leaders of Israel, "…the land has been subdued before the LORD and His people." He also says the LORD has granted them rest on every side. He's pointing to what has already happened, and now it's time to build.

David did say it, friend. He tells the leaders of Israel that the LORD "…has given the inhabitants of the land into my hand, and the land has been subdued before the LORD and His people." He says the LORD has also granted them rest on every side.

That's it, friend. David wants them to bring "…the ark of the covenant of the LORD and the holy articles of God into the temple that will be built for the Name of the LORD." The temple is built for the ark and the holy articles. David is looking all the way to the finished house.

The bronze serpent is in the Bible (Numbers 21:9), but David doesn't mention it here. He wants the ark of the covenant of the LORD and the holy articles of God brought into the temple. Those are the things he names (1 Chronicles 22:19). The serpent isn't on his list.

I admit that's a fun one to guess. But David doesn't mention any sword in these verses. He says the temple is for the ark of the covenant of the LORD and the holy articles of God. That's the plan he lays out for the house of the LORD.
